1:
Most readers fix the psalm to a single crisis. Clarke and Calvin refer it to the confederacy against Jehoshaphat, and Clarke lists his reasons: the Ammonites and Moabites were the principal movers, the Edomites assisted, the coalition drew in strangers from Syria and beyond the sea, and the chronicler names a prophet of the race of Asaph — quite possibly the Asaph named in this title. Calvin concurs, matching the psalm's roll of nations against the chronicler's. Delitzsch, noting this is the last of the twelve Asaph psalms, reports a competing case for the Maccabean age: hostility breaking out on every side against a people newly independent and doubly self-conscious after the dedication of the temple explains the psalm, he thinks, far better than the efforts to obstruct the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Augustine goes past occasion altogether. Asaph, he says, means congregation — in Greek, synagogue — so the name stands for the assembled people of God; and he takes the opening question of Christ, reckoned in his humiliation comparable to other men, even to the robbers crucified beside him, but of whom, when he comes in glory, none shall ask who is like him.

On the silence itself the comment is uniform and vivid. Gill defines it as God not answering his people's prayers, not pleading their cause, not rebuking their enemies. Henry pictures God conniving at the unjust treatment of his people, holding his peace as though observing an exact neutrality, sitting by as a man astonished or a mighty man that cannot save — then draws the comfort out of the complaint, since God's speaking is his acting, saying and doing being with him the same thing. He notices too that a prayer offered in great distress is still called a song, for singing psalms is not unseasonable even when the harps hang upon the willow trees. Spurgeon presses the contrast between noise below and quiet above: man is clamorous, be not thou speechless; he rails and reviles, wilt not thou reply? The appeal is to the Mighty One, and the psalmist asks not for a leader bold and brave nor for any human force but casts the whole burden on God. Ellicott adds only the phrase's literal shape: God, not silence to thee. Calvin reads the doubled plea as urgency confessed: it is our duty to wait patiently when God delays, but in condescension to our infirmity he permits us to beg him to make haste.

The enemies are drawn with the same energy. Ellicott notes that their tumult is literally a roaring like the sea, so rendered in the Greek and Latin, and the crafty counsel literally a plot made crafty. Spurgeon hears a hungry pack of dogs all giving tongue at once, shouting already over the feast they are sure of; their pride is a brass that always sounds. Gill traces the subtlety to the king of Egypt's dealings with their forefathers and behind that to the old serpent, but remembers that the wise are taken in their own craftiness. Clarke supplies the geography — the invaders had entered Judea and encamped by the Dead Sea — and the scale: eight or ten nations bound in one purpose to exterminate the race so that no record should remain, the plan kept so secret that the king heard nothing until his territories were overrun. Never, was Judah in greater danger. Over the intended victims the readings part. Wesley and Ellicott take the hidden ones as the people, God's peculiar treasure under his close protection; Henry agrees, adding that whoever destroys a man's children and ruins his estate is fighting the man himself. Clarke canvasses the versions, which give thy holy ones, thy saints, and the hidden things in thy treasures, and allows the phrase may point not to the people but to the temple, the ark and its stores.
5:
The word behind confederate is a butcher's word. Clarke and Ellicott both note that the Hebrew says they have cut a covenant, and Clarke spells out the rite: an animal slain, divided, and the parties passing between the pieces. Spurgeon takes the ratifying blood as the measure of their resolve — men banding to make war on the Mighty God, aiming at him through the sides of his saints. Ellicott draws it the other way: God and his hidden ones are one, a truth preparing for the later identification of the Son of man with everyone needing help or pity. Gill notes only that men agreeing in nothing else agree in this. The roll of nations is read genealogically by Spurgeon, geographically by the rest. Edom is nearest of kin yet first in enmity, the sire having despised the birthright and the sons despising its possessors; the Ishmaelites keep up the grudge between the bondwoman's child and the freewoman's; Moab is born of incest yet still a kinsman, whose seed Lot could never have dreamed would prove such enemies. Ammon and Amalek he leaves detestably immortalised in the roll of infamy — how thick they stand.

Clarke explains why they are counted by their tents: several of these peoples, the Ishmaelites especially, kept a migratory life. He places the Hagarenes east of Gilead and identifies Gebal with the Giblites, an unconquered Canaanite tribe of stone-squarers who prepared timber for the temple. The Philistines, he adds, had been tributaries to Jehoshaphat and turned on him; Tyre joined hoping to extend its territory. Gill locates Gebal in Phoenicia near Tyre; Wesley makes it an Arabian people on the southern edge of Canaan. Ellicott unsettles the entry: if it is a noun it must be a synonym for Edom, the Phoenician Gebal not to be thought of — but most likely it is no noun at all, and the line should read that Ammon and Amalek are joined together, the Philistines with the men of Tyre. He is equally unwilling to let the last name stand: the form is Assyria, but some take it for Syria, so that a later kingdom may be honoured here by a grander and more ancient name. Gill reports and rejects a reading that would date the war after Hezekiah.

The precedents pleaded are two old routs. Henry treats the prayer as prophecy — whoever opposes the kingdom of Christ may read his doom here — and grounds it on the unchangeableness of God, the same to his people and against their enemies. Midian, he notes, was routed by its own fears more than by Gideon's three hundred, the corpses lying like dung spread to fatten the ground — a precedent Deborah herself fixed for aftertimes. Spurgeon says faith delights to light upon precedents and quote them before the Lord, the nations then much the same and the plight similar; when God wills it a brook can be as deadly as a sea, Kishon as terrible to Jabin as the Red Sea to Pharaoh. He turns the figure into a judgement: those who would not give Israel a place above ground were denied a hiding place under it, and having counted God's people dung, became dung. Delitzsch supplies the mechanism, the Kishon carrying away the corpses, and places En-dor near Tabor within the battlefield. Over that name the readers divide: Clarke refers it to Gideon's defeat of Midian in Jezreel, Gill and Delitzsch to the destruction of Jabin and Sisera, and Ellicott observes that the Judges account never mentions the place. Henry adds why the princes are named separately: the common people would not have been so mischievous had their leaders not set them on. Spurgeon agrees — smite the great ones too, and suffer not the ringleaders to escape. Ellicott ends on the boast, preferring pastures to houses in what the confederates claimed.
13:
The wheel is the psalm's most contested image. Wesley takes it simply: men promising themselves a sure possession are wished the instability of a thing soon removed. Henry works it both ways — continual motion, giddy in all their counsels, rolling down speedily to their own ruin; or the threshing wheel that beats out corn. Those who trust God have their hearts fixed; those who fight him are unfixed like a wheel. Clarke commits to the threshing floor: the broad wheel rolled over grain in the open air, the chaff carried off as the grain is thrown up against the wind. Gill records it but prefers another: the word means a rolling thing before the wind, a wisp of straw or thistledown. Ellicott makes the same case at length, noting the term is rendered elsewhere as a rolling thing, with thistledown in the margin and dust of a wheel in the Greek, and identifying it with the wild artichoke — vegetable globes, light as a feather, which become the sport of the wind when the parent stem breaks. The region still curses by it: may you be whirled like the weed before the wind.

Fire follows wind. Gill notes how swiftly a forest goes up once kindled: wicked men are no more to God's wrath than trees of the forest. Wesley confines the burning mountains to their woods, which in hot countries burn with irresistible violence. Clarke keeps the threshing floor even here: since floors were often sited on hills to catch the wind, the burning mountains may be the chaff burnt after winnowing. Henry presses the sequence: driven stubble rests at last under some hedge, so the prayer is that they be not driven away only, but burnt up. The storm he reads as raising terror in the sinner's own heart, so that God can make the proudest defier of his justice afraid as a grasshopper — the torment of devils is that they tremble. Clarke pauses to defend the run of curses. He sets them against the ancient custom of pouring execrations on an enemy before battle, and insists none of these words touches the enemies' souls or their eternal state, only their discomfiture now. Were the powers of the continent to combine against Britain, he asks, what Christian would not meet them so? On the knees of his soul he would offer every one of these petitions against such invaders.

The closing verses turn the curse towards a purpose. Henry states it plainly: what we should beg for persecutors is that God bring them to repentance, desiring no confusion for them but such as may be a step towards conversion — let them be put to a stand, with leisure to consider what an unequal match they are. Delitzsch agrees the aim is that they lay hold of mercy in the middle of their downfall, escaping utter destruction only by giving God the glory; and he refuses to limit the knowing at the end to a perception of the punishment's justice, since knowledge unto salvation is not excluded. Spurgeon grants that shame has often weaned men from their idols; but where men remained obstinate he thinks justice rightly invoked — what else could be done, and better they perished than that Israel be rooted up. Gill glosses the shame as disappointment rather than penitence, noting a rendering that fills their faces with fire, as a man's face burns when deeply confounded. On the final name they part again. Gill takes it as expressing being, eternity and unchangeableness, excluding not the Son or Spirit but every fictitious deity. Spurgeon has the heathen compelled to acknowledge a greatness they denied. Ellicott sees more: the nations were to seek him not merely as God but as the God of Israel, and looking back we may read a grander hope still, of nations united in believing the common fatherhood of God.
